speechtext: This bill refers to the refinancing of the Central Vermont which is a subsidiary of the Canadian National Railways. As this railway is located wholly in the United States, I think it is due to the house and to the country that the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Crerar) should state the situation with relation to it and tell us how much of the public moneys of Canada is invested in it. subtopic: LOAN OF $8,609,000 TO RETIRE CENTRAL VERMONT REFUNDING MORTGAGE BONDS
speechtext:
The object of the bill was discussed by myself very fully when it was in the resolution stage, but I will be glad to give the committee the information asked for by the hon. member. The Central Ver-

mont railway was under the control, by stock ownership, of the old Grand Trunk Railway of Canada, the majority of the stock having been secured, as my memory serves me, well over thirty years ago. That relationship continued until the Grand Trunk was taken over and incorporated in the Canadian National system. In 1920 the Grand Trunk had to provide for certain maturing obligations amounting to $12,000,000, which was done by guarantee of the Grand Trunk, given by its board of directors, as to principal and interest of the bonds of the Central Vermont. In 1920 *there were disastrous floods in the state of Vermont and the Central Vermont railway, along with other railways in that state, suffered very heavy losses. Steps were taken by the Canadian National Railways, who were then operating the Central Vermont, to have it put into the hands of a receiver, and the railway remained in that condition until January of the present year when the receivership was discharged. When the road went into receivership it was necessary, under the terms of the mortgage securing the bonds which had been guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway in 1920, for the Canadian National Railways to take up those bonds, which were then outstanding tio the amount of $8,609,000. This matter was provided for through temporary financing, and the object of this bill is to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian National Railways and thus clear up the matter. In January of this year the road was purchased from the receiver by the Canadian National Railways for $22,000,000, and in addition to that there were outstanding $5,000,000 of receiver's certificates. As far as my information goes, that is the story of the adventure of the old Grand Trunk in the Central Vermont railway. Bonds of the Central Vermont railway will be issued and deposited with the Minister of Finance and will remain under his control and direction.

In regard to section 3 (a), might I ask the minister to consider extending that exemption of $500 to at least two collateral cases? An exemption of $500 to a man who takes care of his brother, sister, father, or mother is appropriate, but is it not more worthy of recognition by the state that a man should take care of his wife's sister and his wife's mother? I suggest that this $500 exemption be extended to the siSter-inlaw and her mother. It is all right for hon. gentlemen to smile. I understand the meaning of the smile. On section I-That the corporation rate of tax be paid in respect of undistributed income when such undistributed income is received by a corporation on the sale or winding up of another corporation.

I direct the attention of the minister to what after all is a technical matter, but inasmuch as we are altering the law in relation to undistributed income, I desire to call his attention to a situation that has arisen. Section 1 reads:
That the corporation rate of tax be paid in respect of undistributed income when such undistributed income is received by a corporation on the sale or winding up of another corporation.
Now if hon. gentleman will refer to section 6 they will see that it states that section 1 shall be deemed to have come into effect at the commencement of the 1930 taxation period. That is, it is dated back to the 1st day of January, 1930. As the resolution stands, the provisions of section 6 make the provision of section 1 retroactive in effect. That is my first objection. Unless care is taken in respect to the question of undistributed income in the bill, this provision will be retroactive to the beginning of time in the case of undistributed income. That is hardly fair.
I wonder if the minister, who of course is familiar with the law, knows that under the present act, section 19, it is provided that on the winding up of a company the distribution of the assets in any form shall be deemed to be the payment of a dividend to the extent that the company has on hand undistributed income. That is to say, on the winding up of a company undistributed income is taxable as such when it goes into the hands of the shareholders. Thus if a company sells its assets for cash and distributes the proceeds to the shareholders, they are taxable to the extent that the balance sheet shows them to be part of earned surplus. That is the law to-day. But the present act provides that dividends paid to an incorporated company by a company incorporated in Canada, the profits of which have been taxed under the act, are not liable to taxation. That is, where the dividends of a company the shares of which are owned by another company are paid to the shareholders of that other company. That is provided by section 4(n) of the present act. It is perfectly legal now for a company, instead of selling its physical assets, to sell its issued capital stock to another company. ing their shares. They then get the total price of their assets including surplus in the form of the price of their stock just as though they had sold their stock individually on the market. The purchasers can then have a new company incorporated to which the shares of the original company are transferred. The new company can then take the assets of the original company, by distribution in winding up, and under the provisions of section 4, paragraph (n) of the present act, the new company is protected from liability to income tax on the earned surplus. It may be said that by that method the shareholders of the selling company escape payment of income tax on undistributed and earned surplus or income; but it is a perfectly legal transaction, and to make this provision that we are now dealing with retroactive is, I submit, wholly unfair.
I can say for the minister's benefit and assistance that I have taken occasion to discuss this matter with the income tax authorities, and while they admit that it bears the construction which I have indicated, they say that it was not the intention of the department to go that far, but to go back only to the 1st day of January, 1930. But unless the bill is properly worded, to provide against the contingency I have mentioned, there will be very grave injustice done.
Even to go back to the beginning of 1930 is, in my opinion, not quite fair because that too has this retroactive feature. I would suggest to the minister that instead of making this retroactive to the beginning of the 1930 taxation period, he provide in the bill that it take effect from the beginning of the next taxation period, the beginning of the 1931 period, or the end of the 1930 taxation period. In that way the government and the department will not be open to the charge of passing retroactive legislation, which on principle is always bad, and which may bear hardly in a given case.
I am not objecting to the principle of the amendment to the act, because in principle an undistributed income has as much right to pay taxation as distributed income, but it has not been made taxable in the past and it has been perfectly legal to do what I have indicated has been done; and to make this provision retroactive now would create an injustice in existing pending cases, and there are cases existing such as I have indicated where the entire issue of capital stock of one corporation is being sold to another and title being taken in a holding company. That is the objection to this legislation. The objec-

tion is chiefly to the retroactive feature. I have no desire to see shareholders escape paying taxation if it is levied in a proper way, but I submit that the department in making this provision retroactive is not proceeding in quite a proper way.
My position is plain. I am quite sure the officers of the income tax branch understand the matter very thoroughly, perhaps much more thoroughly than I do myself. I think if the minister will consult them they will agree with me that the abjection is to the retroactive feature and not to the principle underlying the taxation in question. If the minister will make this effective from the beginning of the next taxation period I do not think anyone can have the slightest objection to it. Those who have transactions pending will not be injured. They have proceeded under the present law, and I do not think it is quite fair that the law should be changed and made to relate back so as to cover pending transactions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The intention of this section of the resolution is to overcome the scheme of avoidance of taxation, which as my hon. friend from YorknSunbury (Mr. Hanson) states, has the benefit of legality at the present time, although certainly the spirit of the law does intend that that taxation shall be paid. A legal method has been found of evading it in this case, and the amendment is designed to prevent that in the future and to ensure that taxation will be paid upon undistributed income of companies when they are absorbed by other companies. My hon. friend is afraid of the retroactive feature?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure him that the bill will not go back of this calendar year; but it is intended to embrace all transactions which take place within this calendar year, which is the year of taxation for all income tax payers. So far as putting its operation forward to the beginning of 1931 is concerned, that would be simply to invite those who have any intention at all of evading taxation under the present law to get their schemes matured in 1930, and I am sure my hon. friend would not want that to happen. I can see no harm whatever in making the amendment apply to the present taxation period.

The minister admits that it would not be right to go back beyond the present taxation period, but I am sure the gentlemen who are sitting with him will agree with me that as the resolution reads it is retroactive as to past years.

Income War Tax Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a matter for the lawyers to settle in the terms of the bill. I can assure my hon. friend that it is not our policy to go back beyond the calendar year.

The minister does not say so in so many words, but he rather suggests that there is something immoral on the part of my profession or of the accountant's profession in studying this act and devising ways and means-not to enable their clients to evade payment of taxation, but to prevent their having to pay taxation. Perhaps I am going a little too far when I say he is suggesting there is something immoral about it.
I think it is quite proper. To my mind it is the duty of a lawyer to point out to his clients their rights under taxation. Undoubtedly it is quite legal to do what is being done to-day and what has been done in the past in this connection. I suggest to him that the immorality-perhaps that is a little too strong a word to use in the premises-consists in making the amendment retroactive. It may be said that there has been a loophole in the law. Well, I assume the law was designed to cover the cases the department had in mind at the time. It has not done so. Now circumstances crop up which suggest a change in the law. With the principle of that I am not finding any fault, because I like to see everybody pay his just share of taxation. But I do object to the retroactive feature, and if the minister will give further thought to the matter I think he will agree with me that it is a very bad principle. It is to be condemned in almost any class of legislation, and in taxation legislation in particular. I have always raised objection to making a tax retroactive. People have gone along, legally, honestly carrying out their business transactions on the assumption of having to pay certain existing taxes. It is a rude awakening for them to find that the legislature by an arbitrary provision- and I am not using the word "arbitrary" in any improper sense-cuts away the ground from under their feet. This amendment is perfectly all right and will receive my support if the minister omits the retroactive feature. I think the minister understands my point fully. I am pleased that the amendment will not be effective beyond this taxation period, but I think he ought to make it apply to the period beginning with 1931. I may say frankly to the minister that I have no clients interested, nor am I personally interested in the matter, but a professional friend of mine who is very much interested has drawn the matter to my attention. Hence these remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not attempt to follow my hon. friend into a discussion whether finding a hole in the law is moral or immoral. The fact of the matter is, as he himself acknowledges, there was a loophole which enabled parties to escape what I believe to have been the manifest intent and spirit of the act, while not its legal intent. Now we are proposing to plug that hole. It was never intended to make the amendment retrotractive so far as past years are concerned. I am not conceding anything to my hon. friend in that particular, because, as I say, it never was the intention. Retrotractive taxation would be decidedly unwise, and I agree with him as to the unsoundness of it. As to the application of it, however, to this taxation period from the first of January 1930, I regret I cannot follow his objection. I think it is quite proper to make the amendment with respect to taxation of undistributed income apply to the whole of this taxation period, which, as hon. members know, commences from the first of January in each calendar year.
The minister has admitted all my major premises, but he refuses to apply them. He admits that retrotractive legislation is bad, almost immoral-I do not know that he uses that word.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Yet he wants to apply that principle to this taxation period. The minister is not consistent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am trying to be just.

I would not say the minister is not trying to be just, but he is not logical, he is not consistent. Of course, I may say that the minister has been open to that charge on a good many occasions in relation to this budget, and this is just one more example of his inconsistency-in fact a very minor one in my judgment. But I do suggest that if he admits the principle for which I contend, then to be logical and to be absolutely just he should have this amended provision take effect, not at the beginning of this year, but at the end.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What I shall now read will not prevent consideration of the point at a later time. Section 4 of the said act is .mended by adding thereto the following paragraphs:
(p) The income of farmers', dairymen's, live stockmen's, fruit growers', poultrymen's, fishermen's and other like cooperative companies and associations whether with or without share capital organized and operated on a cooperative basis, which organizations-
(a)	market the products of the members or shareholders of such cooperative organizations under an obligation to pay to them the proceeds from the sales on the basis of quantity and quality less necessary expenses and reserves'
(b)	purchase supplies and equipment for the use of such members under an obligation to turn such supplies and equipment over to them at cost, plus necessary expenses and reserves.

Such companies and associations may market the produce of, or purchase supplies and equipment for non-members of the company or association provided the value thereof does not exceed 20 per centum of the value of produce supplies or equipment marketed or purchased for the members or shareholders.
That means that any cooperative organization falling within the groups there mentioned or other like groups may do business for its own shareholders provided that the arrangement of the business is to return all proceeds less the necessary reserves and expenses to those who contribute the commodities or, in the second place, in the case of the purchasing association, to those who purchase the goods.
The question arises as to how we shall decide as to the qualifications, because to a limited degree some of these organizations do business with other than their own members. We could not say that it would cease to qualify because it sold or bought from one person who was not a member, and it was decided that 20 per cent of the value would represent a fair dividing line. Any organization which does SO per cent of its business with its own members under the plan of returning to its members the whole proceeds less expenses and reserves will qualify for exemption from income tax. Any organization which does more than 20 per cent of its business with those other than its own members will not qualify.

I do not object to the principle of exemption as applied to the purely cooperative associations. I think it would be as fair to exempt such associations as it is to exempt provincial commissions such as the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario. There is a very strong feeling in certain sections of the country that this commission should not be exempted, especially where it operates in competition with privately owned corporations. I have no doubt that to a lesser degree there is the same feeling with respect to cooperative companies. I do not think however that the same principle is applicable where they are trading outside of their own immediate constituencies. I would be curious to know why the arbitrary figure of 20 per cent was taken; it seems to me that as these cooperative companies grow they spread out and make money; they become trading corporations and in principle they cease to be cooperative associations. Where they become purely merchandizing companies and the cooperative principle is disregarded, they ought to pay income tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

The only qualification is that they must do 80 per cent of their business with their own members, and return to those members a certain amount on a commodity basis, less expenses and reasonable reserves. I must say that it was difficult to arrive at the figure of 20 per cent. I was interviewed by representatives of cooperatives from coast to coast. The cooperative movement operates in a variety of ways; there are different bases of operation. For instance, the dairy men of the Fraser valley have a very prominent cooperative organization, and it differs entirely from those of the wheat pools or cattle pools of the prairies. As a matter of fact, the cattle pools differ from the wheat pools. For this reason it was necessary to find some common ground upon which all of those essentially bona fide cooperative organizations could be dealt with without at the same time paving the way for the incorporation of what might be called bogus cooperatives created for the purpose of evading the income tax. I do not think there is any danger in the 20 per cent leeway, because no bogus organization could possibly gain anything. It would have to do 80 per cent of its business with its own members or shareholders, and it would have to return to them the whole of the commodity value less operating expenses and reserves. In that arrangement there would be no temptation to create bogus cooperatives to evade the tax. I have given considerable personal study to this matter, and I am satisfied that the provision I have stated will meet the requirements of the case. There was only one exception, and that was the difficulty which arose in connection with certain cooperative banks in the province of Quebec which undoubtedly are of a truly cooperative nature, and are causa populi. The bill will provide for the exemption of such institutions. I doubt very much whether they would have to pay an income
tax in any case under the present law, because they do not have profits. Being purely cooperative institutions they should come within the scope of the exemptions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the committee
rose at one o'clock we were considering subsection (b) of section 3 of the Income War Tax Act.

The minister
was kind enough to say that he would leave the door open in considering suggestions made with reference to this subsection. May I put on record a somewhat similar provision in the United States income tax legislation dealing with this subject. It exempts contributions or gifts made within the taxable year to or for the use of:
any corporation or trust, or community chest, fund, or foundation, organized and operated exclusively for religious, charitable, scientific, literary, or educational purposes, or for the prevention of cruelty to children or animals, no part of the net earnings of which inures to the benefit of any private shareholder or individual.
It will be seen that that exemption from income tax of contributions or gifts is much wider in its scope than in this subsection. I think I have made it perfectly clear that I have no objection to the exemption from income tax of donations to churches and other religious institutions. All I am asking the minister to do is to extend the provision to cover donations to charities and social agencies, which apparently have been excluded, for administrative reasons. The Federated Charities of Montreal is an outstanding example of an organization such as I have in mind. It collects about three quarters of a million dollars annually for some thirty charitable institutions in the city. It is very efficiently managed and is doing very valuable work. I should think it would be no more difficult for the income tax authorities to administer the act with regard to donations to this and similar institutions than it would be with respect to donations to churches, colleges, universities, hospitals and the other institutions covered by the subsection under discussion. Unless the scope of this amendment is extended as suggested I fear it will discourage contributions to charitable and 2419-15*i
social organizations, to the detriment of the very necessary work that they carry on in our large cities. This would very adversely affect such splendid institutions as the Victorian Order of Nurses, the Child Welfare Association, the Mental Hygiene Committee, the Children's Aid Society, the Family Welfare Association, the social settlement of boys' and girls' clubs, the Social Hygiene and AntiTuberculosis Association, the Red Cross Society, and so on. As most of these organizations are operating under a federal or a provincial charter, I do not think there would be any difficulty of administration involved if they were brought within the scope of this subsection. I would point out to the minister that the province of Quebec has recently amended its inheritance tax legislation to exempt from taxation legacies to certain associations, amongst which are the charitable institutions I have enumerated.

Mr. Chairman, I recognize that this subsection includes universities, but could it be interpreted as embracing such institutions as are essentially educational in their nature-for example a museum? It is conceivable that by a narrow interpretation of the words " university, college, school," such museums might be excluded from the benefits of the provision. I have a specific oase in point-a provincial museum. I think the purpose of the subsection is admirable, but I should like to know if it will be interpreted in a liberal sense to cover museums, they being in their character essentially educational institutions. If not, I would suggest that the subsection be amended to effect this purpose.

speechtext: The old rates were one-tenth of one cent on shares of 50 cents and under; oner-quarter of one cent on shares between 50 cents and $1. The new rate on all shares less than SI will be crae-tenith of one per cent, calculated on the money total of the transaction, instead of the fixed rate of one-tenth of one per cent on the share value. That will cut the tax down very materially indeed. On shares from $1 to $3 the old rate was one cent; the new rate is one-quarter of one cent per share from SI to S5. The old rate on shares between $3 and $20 was two cents per share; the new rate is one cent per share on shares from $5 to $25. The old rate was three cents per share on shares between $20 and $100; the new rate is two cents per share on shares from $25 to $50, three cents on shares from $50 to $75, and four cents on shares from $75 to $150. On shares over $100 the new rate is four cents, and on shares over $150, five cents.

I might add to the minister's statement by giving some instances of the reductions as applied to certain companies. I have here a schedule which has been worked out for me by a reliable accountant, and I submit it as being approximately correct. The schedule covers thirty companies and shows a reduction from the old tax of 33 per cent on the shares of such companies as Noranda and International Nickel, increasing in the case of the penny stocks up to as high as 98 per cent reduction of the old tax. For instance, in Thomson-Cadillac the old tax has been reduced 96 per cent. The so-called penny stocks are reduced from 64 to 99 per cent. The average reduction might be said to be 75 per cent. In the higher priced stocks the reduction is from 33 per cent up to 50 per cent. The tax on Hollinger, for instance, selling at the present market price of $6.55, is reduced by one-half, while on Teck-Hughes selling at about the same price, $6.75, there is a similar reduction. I think that is a fair statement of the general application of this new schedule.
There is another matter that I would bring to the attention of the committee. It has to do with the question of the share tax in Canada as compared with the share tax in the United States. In that connection, exclusive of provincial tax I find that a stock such as Hollinger, selling at a price of $6.55 per share, carries a tax on a sale of one thousand shares in New York of $2, while the tax in Canada under this new schedule is $10.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does that $2 include the state tax in New York as well as the federal?

I understand so. It does
not include the provincial tax in this country. The $2 is the tax if the deal was made on the New York stock exchange. The other figure is exclusive of the provincial tax in this country. If my figures are correct, it would appear that the tax on a purchase of Hollinger in New York would be less than 25 per cent of the tax which would be charged on the purchase of the same number of shares in Montreal or Toronto. The point I want to put before the minister is whether by this tax we are not driving certain business to the New York stock exchange to the disadvantage of our own Canadian exchanges. I know that in my own city those connected with the stock exchange business feel that the taxes have already driven a great deal of business to 'Seattle. I am glad that the Minister of Health is now in his seat. As a matter of fact, this is just one of the instances in which the Vancouver Sun, which hon. members know is a pronounced Liberal organ, charges the Minister of Health-he was the sole survivor of the last political wreck there -with the distribution of patronage in order that he might retain his seat. I think the transaction before us affords very fair substantiation of that charge. The facts are-the present Minister of Public Works, of course, does not know them-that the Minister of Health had a political friend who wanted to make a little ready money, and the Minister of Health, who goes on the public platform in British Columbia, tells the people that nothing can be done in or for British Columbia without his recommendation. When did the

In the city of Nelson. I

Mr. KING (Kootenay)): Never; no such statement was made.

I cheered, yes. The facts are just about like this, and I leave it to the house to judge the case. The minister had a political friend in Cranbrook, and that friend wanted to unload something on the government and so he sold them three lots for $5,500 on the recommendation of the Minister of Health, who had an order in council put through. Next year a vote for the construction of a building was put in the estimates. When it was known that the building was to be erected on the site purchased, the people of Kimberley, independent of party, Liberal and Conservative alike, all wired in protest to Ottawa against the construction of a public building on this site for the reason that the location was unsuitable, objectionable and away from the centre of the Itown. Now, $5,500 was spent for a site which was recommended by the minister, a site which was unsuitable and objectionable. It must be taken for granted, in view of that fact, that the minister's judgment of real estate is just about as poor as his political judgment. But the fact is that this property for which he paid $5,500 at the time of the purchase was actually assessed for $850. Let me emphasize that- $850 was the assessed value of the property that the minister recommended should be purchased by the government at $5,500. The people of the town objected, and it was only because there happened to be the end of a blind street available that the minister was able to make an exchange with the then provincial government, which was of the same political complexion as his own. That, in my opinion, bears out the charges in the Vancouver Sun that the Minister of Health merely uses his position for the distribution of patronage in British Columbia in order that he may retain his seat. I extend to the minister from British Columbia the very timely and courteous suggestion that if he has a chance to slip into the Senate by the grace of the Prime Minister he had better take advantage of it.

I can see no appropriation in the estimates for an addition to the New Westminster post office. That matter has been discussed before in this house, and the addition is badly required. The business done in the office warrants the expenditure. When .the Postmaster General visited New Westminster he promised that we would get the addition; he said that it was absolutely necessary, and as a result, I believe on the ground of urgent necessity he recommended the expenditure. He made that statement in this house last session. The Minister of Public Works came along with his broadaxe and slashed it off. I now ask the hon. gentleman why he took that action. The Minister of Public Works and the Postmaster General have no doubt received communications from the Board of Trade, the city council and other organizations in New Westminster [Mr. Eslinjr.)
urging the absolute necessity for the construction of this addition. I know as a matter of fact that the business of the post office is seriously embarrassed at the present time, and in the busy seasons the present facilities are entirely inadequate. It is not necessary to buy a new site. The site is there; it is simply a case of erecting an addition which would not entail the expenditure of very much money. I remember of course that when the 'Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) was in British Columbia he told the people that their difficulty arose from the fact that they did not elect enough Liberals.
Hear, hear.
That seems to be the policy under which the Minister of Public Works is proceeding.
Why?

I wish to tell those
hon. gentlemen that the people in New Westminster, irrespective of their politics, are interested in this matter. They are not particularly anxious to spend the money, but they recommend the expenditure because they feel it is an absolute necessity. I would like to hear an explanation from the Minister of Public Works .as to why he lopped off the 'amount which was recommended by the Postmaster General.

I would like to say that
if my hon. friend has not been able to find in these estimates the item to which he refers, 'I am afraid it as not there; that is the best explanation I can give as to why he has not been able to find it. Representations have been made to the department in regard to the needs in New Westminster, as they have been made in regard to many other places throughout the Dominion.

By the Postmaster
General?

Many recommendations
have been made by the Postmaster General which we have not been able to meet. When my hon. friend referred to the fact that the Minister of Public Works wielded a big axe he gave evidence of the fact that he does not know the Minister of Public Works as well as the Minister of Public Works might wish. For the information of the hon. gentleman I would like to say that the big axe is wielded by four men on the treasury board, and sixteen other men in the council. The result has been that many buildings which the Minister of Public Works considered necessary have not been erected, so that expenditures

The Minister of Public Works seems to be in a humorous mood this afternoon, and his followers seem to think that he has been very clever.
He has.

I do not have to prove it; he admits it. He may be very clever, and it may be all right for this government to preach economy, but I want to tell the hon. gentleman' that the people out at the coast know what is happening in other parts of Canada. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will not feel so happy after the elections; I do not believe he will.

Oh, I hope to feel much

capacity at that terminal?

In 1928 when the minister made the decision in the house, he coupled with that the statement that this was being done on condition that the United States paid its share of the work in the preparation of the river. Has the minister received any assurance that the United States will do so?

The United States now

When the minister made that statement in regard to this selection he knew then, and he also knew when the work began, that he had not the consent of the United States. In July, 1928, the United States absolutely refused to carry out the program and I do not know what influences have been at work to secure even the small grant of $180,000. Will the minister tell us that he is sure of that $1,000,000?

In 1928, when that statement was made, there was an appropriation in the United States harbours and rivers bill providing for this work, oven to the extent of doing $65,000 worth of work in Canadian waters if the Canadian government did not feel disposed to do it. However, there were certain delays with regard to having the bill passed upon by congress, and a new bill was introduced a short time ago, just at the last session, making provision for the work in this channel.

At the time their harbours and rivers bill was presented to congress; it was prior to the time 'that our estimates were being considered. If I remember correctly, there was a distinct understanding-

I did not make that statement.
I have that statement right here.

My hon. friend will find that the statement I made was that if satisfactory arrangements could be made with the United States regarding their portion of the channel, and those arrangements are being carried out.

The hon. minister stated that an amount was included in their estimates, at the time our estimates were being prepared. In July, 1928, you had received an absolute refusal, and no statement to that effect was made in the house. We asked for the papers in connection with this matter, but we were told that because they contained important matters the minister did not desire to lay them on the table. Those papers have since been laid on the table and they do not contain anything which would have prevented their being brought down at that time. Until a few weeks ago the United States had given an absolute refusal to carry on this work. The hon. minister knew that at the time.
I know my hon. friend desires to be absolutely fair, but I think he is under a misapprehension when he makes the statement that there was a refusal on record at the time.
I would ask that this item stand over until I bring the file down.
I shall be very glad to do that.

I will read the
statement of your engineers.
If there is any objection, I shall be very glad to allow the item to stand so that my hon. friend may read the files.
I have the files in my office.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No, I object to the item carrying, unless you intend to force it through.
I think my hon. friend will agree as to the necessity of this vote being put through. I will undertake to produce all the information, but I would suggest that he first allow the vote to go through.

I do not require any information, I have it myself. That file contains communications from the engineers dated July, 1928, saying that the United States had turned down the proposition. I would not stop public works from going on, but I want to make the statement that I do not think the minister has played fair in this matter. We accepted his word that there were certain reasons why the papers could not be brought down, but since that time the papers have been secured and they contain nothing of the nature intimated by the minister. We accepted this proposition at that time on the understanding that the United States was going to do its share of the work in order to enable large boats to come down to this terminal. I submit that the minister was most unfair when he said that there were reasons which prevented these papers being submitted to the house.

I have known my hon friend for many years, and I know that there is no hon. member of this house who is more desirous of being fair. However, if he looks up Hansard he will see that the statement was made that no objection would be taken to my hon. friend or any other hon. member of this house looking at the correspondence, but that I did not think it advisable at that time to have it laid on the table.

I will admit that the minister went just that far and said that if we wanted to force it we could look at the correspondence. I do not intend to prevent the progress of any great public work simply because my own constituency is concerned, but I contend that the decision was based on very unfair grounds. I do not claim that Kingston had everything in its favour, but the decision was made most unfairly. In 1928 the matter was left in abeyance because of the rush of closing, but this year the papers were brought down and they contain no valid reason for the minister's refusal to table them when requested. One of the large steamship companies has objected to going

speechtext:

speechtext:
The Department of Agriculture was mentioned, but as the Minister of Labour is leaving the city for a day or two, it would be preferable, if my hon. friends agree, to take up his estimates next.
DEPARTMENT OF LABOUR Labour-Annuities Act, $75,000.

I remember some years ago
this matter was under consideration and it was then hoped that the cost of annuities might be made a little less to those seeking to purchase them. The present minister may not have any record of what took place then, but at the time hopes were held out that some benefit would accrue along that line. Is there any hope that the cost of annuities to those seeking to purchase them may be reduced?

The information I get from the
experts is that owing to the increased length of life, there is an idea that we ought to increase the cost of annuities instead of decreasing it. At the present time no company can compete with the government in regard to annuities. There is at present no thought of decreasing the price.

I remember at that time the
financial position showed that some money was being made by the government. It was then freely admitted that it was not the desire of the government to make money by the scheme, but that the government wished, if possible, to furnish annuities at cost with perhaps a reasonable reserve against unforeseen contingencies. It would be interesting to the committee to have a statement from the minister as to the annual receipts, disbursements and surpluses.
{Mr. A. E. Hobs.]
What has been the increase in the expectancy of life in the last three or four years?
I have not under my hand the information with regard to the increased length of life, but I think all insurance companies claim that the length of life is increasing. I am glad to know that too.
They are not increasing the premiums.
Did my hon. friend wish a statement showing the number of annuities that are being sold to-day as compared with previous years?	[DOT]

Unfortunately I did not know that this was coming up or I might have looked up the debate of the year to which I refer. It was about six to eight years ago that this very feature was under discussion in the committee. It was then clearly shown that the department was making money and those in charge at that time were of opinion that if that situation continued there would be a possibility of reducing the cost of the annuities. Y e have had, I believe, no further statement in regard to the matter since then. If the minister can give reasons why there is no chance of reducing the cost but on the other hand a chance of increasing it, we would be interested in having them.

I shall be glad to give
my hon. friend a statement on Monday. It has been represented by the head of the insurance department that in the long run we shall probably lose rather than make money by this scheme. I have not the information at hand because I had not expected that this question would come up.

I do not want to press for
something the minister cannot supply. Apparently he has before him nothing to show the receipts and disbursements and whether or not the selling of annuities is profitable. If it is not profitable, it goes without saying that the cost should be increased; if it is profitable, the cost should be reduced.

Is sufficient care being
taken by those who are selling annuities to acquaint the applicants with all the details? There had come to my notice a case where an annuity was sold by the department, and the applicant, after paying premiums for a number of years, found that it meant something altogether different from what he thought at first. Is this phase of the question carefully watched?

Supply-Labour-Annuities

Of course I have no
knowledge of anyone misrepresenting an annuity to anyone. If I had, I should be glad to take the matter up, but I cannot understand why anyone should make misrepresentations. There might be some cases of misunderstandings. When we advertise annuities we ask that prospective applicants apply to the department for information, and we issue pamphlets giving the fullest information possible.

Does this amount of $75,000
represent the cost of administering the Annuities Act?

It includes everything,
such as advertising, commissions, except, of course, the salaries of the permanent staff.

What is the amount of the
total premiums received per annum?

Is the minister able to give me the information now, or does he want the item to stand? I am absolutely in favour of government annuities; I think we should do everything we can to encourage them. I am glad to see that in connection with the Income War Tax Act there is to be an exemption of $5,000 in this connection. We want to do all we can to encourage the buying of annuities, but what I am anxious to see is that they should be made a little cheaper to the public. We cannot exercise any proper judgment if the minister is unable to give us information as to the extent of the business, the receipts, the disbursements and the reserve that is necessary to take care of future liabilities, having regard to the expectation of life and so on. These items are essential to an intelligent discussion of the subject.
I think I can give all information required except that.
Except what?

Information from the head of the insurance department representing that we are selling our annuities too cheaply; that we ought to increase the price in order to cover overhead expenses and things of that sort. I shall be glad to give that in detail on Monday. The statement is a lengthy one.

If that be the case, the situation has absolutely changed since discussion in the house when, if I remember correctly, the Hon. James Murdock was Minister of Labour. If that be so, we ought to know it because it is rather serious. Will the item stand so far as that information is concerned?
If the hon. member insists, we shall have to let the item stand.

Will the minister give
us the comparative cost of government annuities with those of a company like the Sun Life? I went into this matter a few years ago and I found I could do better with companies like the Sun Life than with the government. If that be the case, it disproves to a certain extent 'the 'statement the minister makes that they are losing money.

There is some information
I desire with regard to this item which the minister may not have with him at present. In volume II of the Auditor General's report, part M-5, I find the following charge:
Amount required to recoup the Annuities branch on account of defalcations by W. J. Fleming, annuities agent at Regina (order in council P.C. 21-436, dated March 13, 1929, $1,282.05.
Can the minister give the details of that now, or does he want it to stand over?

I can give them now, but the question will probably be raised again. It was just a case where a man sold some annuities, collected the premiums and forgot to turn in the money, retaining it himself. We followed him until we found him, and prosecuted, with the result that he went to gaol.
Was there no security?
No.
That is just the point I want to follow up. Was this man not bonded by the department?
No.

I asked the minister a question earlier in the session and in reply he told me that he had made a return as required by the act of his officials who were bonded. I have that return. I have read it, and there is not a single official of the Department of Labour named in it, notwithstanding the fact that the minister said that that information would be in the return. I want to know what explanation the minister has for making an answer of that kind. I have the return here and will send it over to the minister if he would like to see it.

The appointment of agents on commission is a new departure in the last few years. We found that people were applying for annuities and nobody was following up these prospects. This particular man was the first one to default. He was not bonded. But after that every agent was bonded. My answer to question No. 4 of my hon. friend was, "No information."

But the minister is required by the act to make a return each year of the

officials who are bonded. I have the return before me, and there is not a single official of the department named in it.
All our permanent officials are bonded.

My question is not whether your officials are bonded. My point is that the minister is not making a return such as he is ordered to make to parliament so that the information may be available to hon. members.
I will let the item stand. Mr. FRASER: The minister will be able to give me more information when it comes up again?

Yes.
Item stands.
Combines Investigation Act, $30,000.

In what state is the
A.B.C. investigation?
It is in the courts now.
How much money was spent on it?
My hon. friend is speaking of the inquiry, not the court procedure?
I was not limiting my question to the courts. I asked how much money had been spent on the investigation.
For the investigation,
That is what was spent last year?
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Administration, Employment Offices' Coordination Act, $17,000.
What has the Department of Labour to do with employment offices? I thought they were largely provincial.
We give them a subvention to help them to carry on.

Item agreed to.
Fair wages and inspection, $15,000.

What are the exact duties that these fair wage officers perform? We had one of them down in Sydney not long ago looking into the wages paid at the steel works. Has the minister received any report or finding from that officer?

Our fair wage officers have nothing to do with private industry. Their business is with public undertakings, to see [Mr. Fraser. 1
that the fair wage policy is carried out, and to investigate any complaints that may be made. There are times, however, when we use these officers as conciliation officers when there is danger of a strike or something of that nature, and they keep us posted how the negotiations are proceeding. Very often they are called upon to act as conciliators in disputes.
How many of these officers are there?
One in the maritimes, one in Montreal, one in Toronto, one in Winnipeg and one in Vancouver.
What territory does the officer in Vancouver cover?
He covers British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan.
With regard to the officer in Halifax, is there some labour trouble down there among the painters? Is the officer taking any part in that dispute, and if so, has he made any report?
That is the only strike we have in Canada to-day, the painters' strike in Halifax, and I hope within the next day or two it will be settled.

Item agreed to.
Administration, Old Age Pensions Act, $10,000.
I understand that when a pensioner under the act has any property he has to make an assignment to the government.

No. There is a provision in the act to that effect, but the federal government has no authority to take property from anyone, and I have been advised that neither does any province administering an old age pension act take property from anyone or require him to transfer it.

A case of that kind was called to my attention by one of the municipal secretaries, who was worried about the taxes on the property which he said had been assigned to the government. I have the assurance of the minister, however, that that is not correct.
Yes.

Item agreed to.
Technical Education Act, $2,000.
What is the significance of this vote of $2,000?

We have to carry on under the act another four years. We had a staff in connection with the $10,000,000 vote for

Supply-Labour
technical education, and this $2,000 is required to enable us to carry on until the balance of the vote is exhausted.
Does that $2,000 cover the cost for the nine provinces?
Yes, for travelling expenses only.

In the Auditor General's report I find a charge for hospital medical care for Mrs. Charles Caucutt, who sustained injuries while attending the employment service council meetings. What are the circumstances justifying a payment of this kind?
She was one of the lady delegates at that meeting, and while here engaged on government business, broke her leg here in the building.

Item agreed to.
Labour-salaries, $269,045; contingencies, $30,000.

How many employees has
the minister in 'the department at present?
There are 136.

The minister is asking
for an increase?
Yes, six.

How many were in the
department when the minister took charge?

I cannot state the exact
number, but we have a few increases owing to the extension of the work of the department, such as old age pensions, annuities, conciliation, and so on. I hope next year to be in a position to ask for a couple more fair wage officers.

There is a departmental
solicitor?
Yes.
Is that a new appointment ?
Yes.

To what extent are the
public taking advantage of annuities?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That item is
held over.	.

What other important
departmental officials have been appointed by the minister?
The minister has not appointed any; the Civil Service Commission has. It appointed the solicitor for the department, the chief conciliation officer, and the fair wage officer in Halifax.
When the position of chief conciliation officer was created by the minister was the senior wage investigator given the position?
No, a new man came in.
What was the justification for bringing in a new man when there was already an experienced officer in the department who had been carrying on the work for years?

It was advertised and
thrown open by the Civil Service Commission. We have got probably one of the best gentlemen in the whole Dominion for the position, as results will show.
What is his name?
Major S. Campbell.

Were his qualifications
superior to those of the men who had been carrying on the work before?

It is not altogether qualifications that count in conciliation work; temperament and experience are the essentials. This gentleman had a great deal of experience in negotiating wage agreements and acting on committees for labour men long before he came here.

Was he appointed over
the heads of the men in the department because he had a wider experience than they?
To my notion the present gentleman has a wider experience than any other officer.

Was that the reason for
his appointment?
Yes.

I notice the minister's
private secretary is getting $4,080, and there is also an allowance of $600.

That is not for the
private secretary; it is the secretarial allowance.

Was there a secretary in
the department when the minister took charge?
Yes.

What were the travelling
and incidental expenses of the minister himself for the year ending March 31, 1930?
About $2,700.
Does that include automobile expenses and all other private expenses of the minister?

That is the amount of
the minister's own private expenses, $2,700.
Including travelling expenses?

All travelling expenses.
Supply-Labour

Chauffeur and automobile
expenses?
No.

I should like to have a
statement including those expenses. My friend suggests aeroplane expenses as well.

The expenditures out of
contingencies for the whole department were as follows:
Salaries	$ 5,203
Travelling expenses,	 4,162
Telephone and telegrams	 7,635
Printing and stationery	 6,874
Sundries	 5,101
Evidently the minister has not understood my question. What was the amount the minister expended in connection with his personal expenses for the year?

I gave my hon. friend
my own personal expenses-$2,700.
Does that sum include the minister's travelling and automobile expenses, and all similar items?

No, it does not include
automobiles; it includes only my personal expenses.
Does it include the minister's travelling expenses?
Yes.

His travelling expenses
were $2,700?
Yes.
Does it include his automobiles, the renewal of his automobiles, repairs, sundries and gasoline?
No, that is additional.
It includes all his travelling expenses?
Yes, in Canada.

In or out of Canada-I
want to have all the information.
Yes.
Yes.

May we have the other
item as to automobile expenses?
That is part of the S2S,000.

Do I understand that the
expenses of the hon. gentleman in connection with the discharge of his duties as Minister of Labour amount to $28,000?
No, no.

What is the cost to the
Dominion of Canada of the Minister of

Labour in connection with the discharge of his duties? That is what I am trying to get.

I can tell the hon. gentleman that there is a salary of $10,000, $4,000 indemnity and $2,700 travelling expenses. I have not the automobile expenses before me. It is all included however in the item of $28,000.

As I understand the minister-
.Some hon. MEMBERS: Carried.

If hon. members insist upon interrupting, they will be here just that much longer. The longer they shout the longer it will take to pass the item. I wish to have a correct answer to my question. May I infer that the minister costs the Dominion of Canada $50,000?
No.

I do not know what my
hon. friend is asking. If there is any information he wishes to have we may go into all the items thoroughly. I may tell the hon. gentleman that it cost the people of Canada $2,700 last year for the travelling expenses of the Minister of Labour, and for that sum he travelled about 40,000 miles, at an average cost of seven cents a mile. He went here, there and everywhere, when any dispute arose. In addition he visited the mines and other places at the request of the miners; he visited different industries to see the conditions under which men were labouring, and in all he covered about 40,000 miles.

I have before me an excerpt from the report of the Auditor General showing the expenditures for the year ended March 31, 1929. In that year the expenditures were as follows: Salary $10,000, indemnity, $4,000, personal expenses, $2,600, minister's automobile renewal, repairs, sundries and gasoline, $2,301, and expenses to Geneva, $6,691, making a total of $25,592. As far as I can learn from the Auditor General's report, that is the answer to the question I have addressed to the minister.

Then why did you
ask it?

The figures I have quoted
are for the year 1929; I want information for the year 1930. Can the minister give me, either now or at some future time, a detailed statement for 1930, to correspond with the one I have given for 1929?

The hon. gentleman
stated that last year the cost was $50,000 Did he multiply by two the expenditures for the year 1928-29?	[DOT]

Questions

No, I did not multiply
anything. I added up the figures which the minister gave me across the floor of the house and the result was very close to S50,000.

Has the hon.
member any objection to that sum of money being spent in the Department of Labour?
No, not at all. I am trying to get an accurate statement of what the Minister of Labour cost this country; I am not objecting to the expenditure in any shape or form.
I would ask the minister to tell us how many strikes there have been in Canada during the last year.

I do not know what that
has to do with it.

I directed my question
to the minister, not to the hon. gentleman across the floor.

Item agreed to.
Progress reported.

Before the house adjourns
I wish ito lay on the table a copy of the convention between Canada and the United States for the preservation of the halibut fisheries of the North Pacific ocean, Behring Sea, signed at Ottawa on May 9, 1930, in respect to the Dominion of Canada, by the plenipotentiary named therein.
